preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: Thanks for kicking this off; I'll take the first concrete design decision on site placement and the accompanying data schema so we have something to iterate on. For our neighborhood site I'm proposing we anchor all primary sensors—temperature, relative humidity, barometric pressure, and a two-component rain gauge—on a single 1.5 m mast positioned at least 10 m from any building roofline, tree canopy edge, or paved surface, ideally over bare mowed grass on a south-facing slope with unobstructed view of the sky in all azimuths, and we treat that mast as our only "reference point" so every reading in the log is traceable to one defined coordinate (latitude/longitude to six decimals, local time zone, UTC offset, and a fixed grid reference we photograph into the record). The record-keeping schema I'm locking in now is a minimal relational structure: an observation table (timestamp in UTC, instrument ID, sensor type, raw value, units, quality flag 0-4, observer initials), an instrument table (make/model/serial, installation date, last calibration date, calibration method, known offset, next-due calibration date), and a site-conditions table (weather at time of reading, wind speed/direction, any anomaly noted, photo reference number), with every row hash-chained daily into a local JSON file that gets mirrored to a shared drive—no one edits a past row, only appends a correction row that cites the original. On the failure side, the concrete danger I want us to engineer around is thermal-inertia bias from a poorly shielded sensor: in a real case a volunteer station in Tucson, Arizona, mounted its temperature sensor on the north wall of a cinder-block garage and never noticed that the July afternoon readings ran 4–5 °C below the co-located NWS Mesonet mast because the concrete radiated stored heat asymmetrically and the sensor's ventilation was partially blocked by a water meter bracket; the bias was smooth and seasonally correlated, so a simple "mean offset" QC pass missed it entirely, and three months of monthly-mean summaries were quietly contaminated before anyone cross-checked against the neighbor station. To prevent exactly that, our protocol mandates a same-day, same-elevation cross-check against at least one nearby public station within 15 km, and any persistent offset exceeding 0.5 °C or 3 hPa triggers a forced recalibration and a site-survey walk before the next observation cycle, logged in the site-conditions table with photos of the mast's immediate surroundings so the record itself becomes the defense against slow, invisible drift.

target.speaker: Y
target.text: Your site specification and the append-only, hash-chained schema are locked in, and I agree the Tucson-style thermal-inertia trap is exactly the kind of slow bias that makes cross-station comparison non-negotiable, so let's now pin down the calibration protocol that your "next-due calibration date" field in the instrument table actually activates. For temperature I'm specifying a two-point check: we ice-point (0 °C) and steam-point (100 °C at local barometric pressure, corrected) the aspirated sensor against a NIST-traceable platinum-resistance reference thermometer at installation, every two months in summer and every three months in winter, and we log both raw reference values and our computed offset into a dedicated calibration-event row in the instrument table so the known-offset field is never a single number but a sliding two-week median; for relative humidity we use two saturated-salt baths—sodium chloride at 75.3 % RH and magnesium chloride at 33.0 % RH at 20 °C—because they require no sealed chamber, just a jar and a lid with a wire seal, and we compare our capacitive probe's reading after it stabilizes (≥20 min in each bath), logging the deviation at each point rather than a single midpoint so we can see whether the sensor is drifting linearly or developing a curvature error; barometric pressure gets a weekly comparison against the NWS station's station-reduced value broadcast on the NOAA site (or, within 5 km, a hand-held aneroid with its own annual NIST certificate) and we accept the comparison only if wind is below 5 m/s and the mast reading is not in a pressure-spike (frontal passage), otherwise the row is quality-flagged 3 and excluded from the offset median; the two-component rain gauge—solid cylinder for liquid, separate tipping bucket for snow—gets a monthly weigh-and-measure audit where we dump the gauge contents into a pre-weighed beaker and verify the collected volume against the number of tips recorded by the datalogger, giving us an absolute volumetric check independent of the tipping mechanism itself. Now the failure I want us to design around specifically: tipping-bucket tip-weight corrosion. In a documented case from a suburban station in coastal Norfolk, Virginia, salt-air ingress into the bucket's pivot housing corroded the small aluminum tip weights over roughly two wet seasons, increasing the effective tipping mass from 0.200 mm-equivalent to about 0.230 mm-equivalent; during any single storm the deficit was roughly 2–3 mm out of a 40 mm event—well inside the station-to-station event scatter of ±5 mm—so the per-event quality flag never tripped, and the only signal was that the station's seasonal accumulated rainfall trailed the NWS station by about 45 mm after sixty-one recorded events, a gap that looked like ordinary orographic undercatch until someone overlayed the two season totals and noticed the discrepancy grew linearly with cumulative rainfall rather than remaining flat; in our protocol the monthly weigh-and-measure audit exists precisely to catch that drift within one or two events of onset, because the measured water volume in the cylinder will disagree with the datalogger's tip count by more than our accepted tolerance of ±2 mm per month, and when it does we open a mandatory recalibration ticket: the bucket is removed, tip weights are weighed against the factory spec on a 0.001 g balance, pivot clearance is inspected under a loupe for pitting, and the event is logged as a site-condition anomaly with a close-up photo of the corroded weights pinned to the instrument table so that the record itself documents the physical degradation rather than leaving a silent, unexplained seasonal deficit that a downstream climate analyst might attribute to a real wet-vs-dry year signal.
